headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: High tides continue flooding Marin County, filling roads and neighborhoods
headlines.description: Thursday, high tides brought floodwaters onto roads, into parking lots, and through neighborhoods throughout Marin County. Elevated water levels were spotted around the county during and after high tide, just after midday Thursday afternoon. These elevated water levels came on what was otherwise a clear day in Marin County. Video footage from the news chopper from that time showed flooding in Sausalito, Belvedere, Mill Valley, Corte Madera, and more. Forecasters say the high tides are compounded by especially warm waters off the Pacific, with thermal expansion of the water leading water levels to rise. Already, officials warned residents of coastal areas to be on alert for flooding this week. Now, the National Weather Service has extended its Coastal Flood Advisory through Sunday at 6 p.m. for low-lying, bayshore locations along the San Pablo Bay, San Francisco Bay, and Monterey Bay. “It’s a little bit alarming, I live right on the marsh,” said Nancy Miller of Mill Valley, who noticed the water level rising at the marsh outside where she lives this week. “Oh yes, I’ve lived here now 9 years, and it’s definitely more than I’ve ever seen,” she said. The high tide flooding prompted Caltrans to close the ramp that connects northbound Highway 101 and Highway 1 in Mill Valley, explained Matt O’Donnell, Marin County Public Information Officer for Caltrans. “They have had to close that same ramp quite a few times this month,” he noted, adding that with El Niño in the forecast for this winter, residents should stay on alert for more possible road closures. O’Donnell noted that drivers who drive into flooded roads risk their own safety and damage to their cars. “It’s just not worth the risk, if a maintenance worker is telling you to stay off that roadway, then stay off that roadway please,” he emphasized. Thursday, Lucky Drive in Corte Madera off of 101 flooded, as it has been known to do during high tides. Officials blocked off parts of the roadway and directed traffic around some of the deeper areas of water. Mary Sackett, Marin County Supervisor for District 1, which covers San Rafael, explained that county workers have been going door-to-door in the Santa Venetia area, asking for access to properties to do flood prevention work. “We really ask that you say yes, and open your door and allow us to do what we can,” Sackett said.

headlines.title: Half Moon Bay's ballot fight over senior farmworker housing
headlines.description: Candido Rosales spent more than 30 years working at flower farms. In retirement, he is still searching for something he can afford: a home where he, his wife and their daughter can live together. Rosales rents a room. His wife and daughter, who recently arrived from Mexico, stay in a separate home with family. “There’s nowhere to live or for all three of us to live together. It’s very difficult,” he said in Spanish. His struggle is part of the debate over Measure Q, which asks Half Moon Bay voters whether to uphold agreements allowing an affordable housing project for senior agricultural workers on city-owned land near downtown. Supporters say the homes would give aging farmworkers a chance to retire with dignity. Opponents question whether the five-story development is the right size for its location. Known as 555 Kelly, the proposal includes 39 income-restricted apartments and one manager’s unit at 535–555 Kelly Ave. The city lists the estimated cost at $41.6 million. Half Moon Bay’s City Council adopted the ordinance approving the agreements with Mercy Housing on May 5. But opponents gathered enough signatures to force a referendum. A yes vote would uphold the ordinance, including a 99-year ground lease at $1 a year. A no vote would reject it. The measure requires a simple majority to pass. If Measure Q fails, the ordinance would not take effect, and the council could not reenact it for one year, according to the city. Belinda Hernandez-Arriaga leads Ayudando Latinos A Soñar, or ALAS, the nonprofit partnering with Mercy Housing on the project. “We have seniors here from 60 and into their 80s working in the field, believe it or not,” she said. Hernandez-Arriaga said farmworkers live in a patchwork of accommodations, including employer-provided housing that charges rent, barracks, trailers, campers and small spaces shared with other families. Some live in their cars, she said. The proposed development would pair apartments with community space and support services. State Sen. Josh Becker, who secured $2 million in state funding for the project, said the 2023 Half Moon Bay mass shooting exposed substandard living conditions at farms. For senior farmworkers who have spent decades doing physically demanding work, Becker said, the development offers a chance for a “safe, dignified retirement.” He also pointed to its proximity to health services and a church as reasons the location makes sense. Opponents say the project’s height could change the downtown’s character. Hal Bogner, who helped organize the referendum through Let Half Moon Bay Voters Decide, said the dispute is about whether the city will remain a place of three-story buildings or move toward taller developments. Opponents also cite traffic, safety and the plan for only 18 on-site parking spaces. They dispute the transit designation used to justify a fifth floor under state density-bonus law. Former Mayor Mike Ferreira said an earlier proposal was only for a four-story building. He criticized the approval of a fifth floor, questioning the transit designation used to justify the added height. Hernandez-Arriaga said the extra height made more sense economically and was not much taller than a building across the street from 555 Kelly Ave. The financing plan relies on county and state grants and loans, along with tax credits, according to the city. Opponents question whether Half Moon Bay could face future costs. Becker emphasized that the project draws on state affordable housing programs. “It’s not funded locally,” he said. “It’s money from the state, it’s money for affordable housing programs.” Under the agreements, Mercy Housing would be responsible for constructing and maintaining the development. It must also meet financing and other predevelopment conditions before entering into the ground lease, according to the city attorney’s impartial analysis. The San Mateo County Farm Bureau opposes the project, arguing that many farmworkers want to live where they work. Bureau President BJ Burns said he houses seven families and that most of his workers want to remain on the farm.”They wanna live where they’re working. The majority of them wanna stay where they’re working”, he said. Longtime flower grower Louie Figone, the bureau’s vice president, said he has been upgrading housing on his property and installing new units. Jeff Regan, an officer with the Yes on Measure Q campaign, questions whether farm owners’ opposition is partly financial, suggesting they see the project as competition for the rental housing they provide at their farms. After opposing the Mercy Housing lease in May, Mayor Debbie Ruddock suggested that the county consider directing money equivalent to the project’s first five years of rent subsidies toward immediate housing on farms. Ruddock, who is seeking reelection, was unavailable for an interview for this report. Both sides point to Stone Pine Cove, an affordable homeownership community built with state funding after the mass shooting, as a successful example of farmworker housing. The ballot fight comes as Half Moon Bay faces a state lawsuit over its housing-planning obligations. Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Department of Housing and Community Development announced the case in July, alleging the city had failed to comply with state Housing Element Law. That law requires local governments to plan for their share of regional housing needs. Approving 555 Kelly would not, by itself, settle that broader case. Nor would a yes vote mean immediate construction. Mercy Housing’s posted schedule anticipates a tax-credit application and construction start in 2027, completion in 2029 and full occupancy in 2030. Those dates are projections. For Rosales, it all comes back to the family he wants to bring under one roof. He described his hope in Spanish: the three of them living together, coming home in peace and having a place to rest.

headlines.title: 2 San Jose police officers arrested, charged after internal investigation
headlines.description: Two San Jose police officers were arrested and charged with evidence tampering and filing a false police report, the department announced Thursday. Raydarius Surry, 29, and Destiney Thompson, 30, are accused of confiscating drugs from someone on the street to replace drug evidence that was lost in another case, according to police. The two are in a relationship and have been with the department for several years – eight for Surry and six for Thompson. Back in August, police launched an investigation into Surry in connection with an arrest he made on May 3. Surry was notified by the department in August that a small baggie containing a small amount of suspected narcotics, which had been listed in his police report, was never booked into evidence, according to police. The baggie was slated to be tested by the county crime lab. On Aug. 12, after being told about the missing evidence, Surry stopped a pedestrian unrelated to the May 3 case and found a similar baggie of suspected narcotics, police said. Surry seized the baggie, did not take any additional enforcement action and later booked the baggie into evidence under the May 3 case number. He did not document the Aug. 12 stop or evidence seizure. Police said Thompson watched body camera footage of the May 3 arrest to allegedly help Surry formulate a plan to replace the missing evidence. “When you take that careless mistake and you conspire to cover it up and plant evidence and create a false police report, now you’re talking about a felony and tremendous erosion of public trust in the department,” legal analyst Steven Clark said. Surry and Thompson surrendered late Wednesday evening and were booked into county jail, police said. They later posted bail and were no longer in custody as of Thursday evening. “Officers are required to maintain the chain of custody without exception and to be completely truthful in their accounts of interactions with the public,” San Jose police Chief Paul Joseph said in a statement. “Falsifying evidence or police reports is a crime, and our Department moved swiftly to remove both officers from duty and pursue criminal accountability. These allegations, if proven to be true, constitute a failure to live up to the standards our community has a right to expect. I will not tolerate any Department member violating the sacred trust placed in us.” Surry was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 2 while the investigation was underway, according to police. Thompson was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 18. Investigators are conducting a thorough review of both officers’ cases, arrests and evidence bookings, the department said. No other discrepancies have been found so far. Silicon Valley De-Bug, a police watchdog group, said the case impacts the department’s credibility. “This is affirming to those that have said that police are not infallible and that they do lie and that they do make up evidence, they plant evidence,” Silicon Valley De-Bug organizer Raj Jayadev said. In a statement, the San Jose Police Officers’ Association said it was deeply disappointed, writing, “If proven true, their actions run counter to the level of honesty and integrity necessary to wear our uniform. The POA will not fund their legal defense…” SJPD referred the case to the California Commission on Peace Officer Standards and Training for temporary decertification review, police said. The police department’s Criminal Investigations Detail referred the criminal investigation to the Santa Clara County District Attorney’s Office, which filed charges Wednesday afternoon.

headlines.title: Family of boy with autism wins countersuit against neighbor in San Jose
headlines.description: A neighbor sued a San Jose family whose son has autism, claiming the child’s grunts in the back were a “nuisance.” The family countersued and, this week, a jury ruled in their favor. Ezequiel, known as Zeke, is a 14-year-old teenager who suffers from Level 3 autism, a severe form of the disorder that sometimes involves loud grunting. “It requires very high support needs. Usually full care with dressing, bathing, toileting, dangers, safety. It’s a lot,” Zeke’s mom Serena Arvayo said. Zeke and his mom lived with her dad in a home in San Jose until a neighbor filed a lawsuit, claiming her property value was dropping because of Zeke, and that she was suffering emotional distress, labeling the child a “nuisance”. That’s a word the family says traumatized them. “It was hurtful. You use that for an animal, or a car alarm that won’t shut off. But not an autistic individual,” Arvayo said. “Completely outrageous. I mean, how can a family intentionally inflict emotional distress on a neighbor because the child was innocently playing in the back yard and making noise? Sounds of joy,” Elizabeth Hansen with Behar Gibbs Savage Paulson, LLP said. Arvayo says it took away Zeke’s humanity. They moved out of her dad’s rental home, so as not to cause more problems, but the neighbor’s lawsuit remained in place. Arvayo then countersued and both suits went to trial. “It’s a challenge. We can’t just live anywhere. An apartment, we won’t live in. Sharing walls is very difficult because we’re always very careful and mindful of other people, but I always now go next door and say ‘Hey, this is my son. If you have any worries, please come talk to me’,” Arvayo said. This week, the Arvayo family won the countersuit. The same jury awarded them $8 million. Arvayo says it gave her son his humanity back. “My son was represented with dignity. And that was the most important thing for him, to have the dignity he deserves,” Arvayo said. “I think the jury in this case was sending a message. That in a civilized society, we need to have empathy and compassion, and civility at its most basic level,” Arvayo’s lawyer Missy Cornejo said. “This delivers a message to people think they can get away with bad behavior. You better be careful because you might pay the consequences,” Arvayo’s lawyer Ron Rossi said. Repeated messages to the plaintiff’s lawyer have not been returned. The Arvayo family now is relieved, hoping Zeke has given other children on the spectrum a voice.

headlines.title: Homes across the Bay Area report thefts of Halloween decorations
headlines.description: This October, thieves are going after Halloween decorations outside of people’s homes around the Bay Area. A surveillance video in San Francisco shows someone in a green hoodie walking by. He seems to spot the inflatables. He grabs them and then walks away with them. “My husband said, ‘Hey, did you move the blow ups inside for any reason into the garage?’ and I said, ‘No, I didn’t,’ he said, ‘I was going to turn them on but I just looked at the Ring camera and someone came at 2 a.m. and grabbed them’,” SF resident Diana Naranjo said. Naranjo says it happened about a week ago. The decorations were her kids’ favorites. “I was like, ‘Oh man, my boys are going to be disappointed’,” she said. “They were the boys specific favorites because it’s Nightmare Before Christmas. It’s our favorite movie, we couldn’t find a replacement.” And she’s not alone. Last week, NBC Bay Area reported about a San Leandro family who said they got their animatronics stolen. There have also been posts online about stolen decorations along the Peninsula and in San Jose. One neighbor posted on social media a few days ago that their animatronic witch was taken from her front yard in Willow Glen. “What these folks do with it really varies, sometimes you have kids who take things just to take things, you have individuals who vandalize things just to vandalize things and now that we’ve evolved into more high tech equipment for both Halloween and Christmas, we’re going to see an uptick in those thefts because they’re highly sale-able,” law enforcement analyst and retired San Jose Police Detective Michael Leininger said. Neighborhoods all over the Bay Area are known for their spooky decor. Now, many neighbors say they take precautions and have cameras keeping a watchful eye over their yards. Experts say that is exactly what they should do. “If they have surveillance cameras, put up a sign that says you’re under surveillance, people do take those seriously,” Leininger said. Last year, theft was also a problem around Christmas. Leininger says these types of incidents can be low priority for law enforcement agencies, but having those cameras can help.

headlines.title: Dog dies after being attacked by two other dogs near Oakland's Lake Merritt
headlines.description: An Oakland woman is speaking out after her dog died following an attack by two other dogs near Lake Merritt on Oct. 23. For 12 years, Pepper was more than just a pet to Tomiquia Moss. She was family. “When your pet grows up with you, they teach you, they are at your every beck and call, they walk with you in the kitchen, they go to the bathroom with you,” Moss said. But a walk near Oakland’s Lakeside Park last Friday changed everything. “That presence is really difficult to have on a Friday morning. You’re walking your dog and then she’s gone,” she said. On Oct. 23, Moss says two large cane corsos ran towards Pepper and violently attacked her, leaving the dog with serious injuries. “They had her entire body, both dogs, shaking her body for at least three minutes before the man go there,” Moss said. Pepper later died from those injuries and Moss claims the dogs’ owner walked away without showing remorse. “This man who had these animals off leash, watched them maul my dog left the scene,” she said. After a witness shared news of the attack online, other dog owners came forward claiming similar encounters with what they believe were the same dogs. Oakland police and animal services confirm they’re investigating reported dog attacks at city parks but have not confirmed any connection between the incidents. Now Moss wants the owner to be held accountable. “I know that this person will be held accountable and there will be justice for Pepper,” she said.

headlines.title: Having kids out of the question for many Bay Area residents due to high cost of living
headlines.description: The cost of living in the Bay Area is keeping many couples from starting a family, according to a recent survey. Of the roughly 1,800 childless adults younger than 50 surveyed by Joint Venture Silicon Valley, with the Bay Area News Group, 56% said they are unlikely to have children and 58% said they can’t afford to raise kids in the Bay Area. “The screaming headline is that people feel hammered in the Bay Area,” Joint Venture Silicon Valley President and CEO Russell Hancock said. “They can’t afford to live here, and it’s getting worse. The main thing that’s upsetting to folks is that housing seems like it’s now completely out of reach.” NBC Bay Area’s Christie Smith has more in the video report above.

headlines.title: Dream defeat Valkyries to force decisive Game 7 in WNBA Finals
headlines.description: Allisha Gray scored 23 points and Rhyne Howard had 21 as the hot-shooting Atlanta Dream held off Golden State’s late rally to take an 80-69 victory over the Valkyries in Game 6 on Thursday to pull even in the WNBA Finals. The decisive Game 7 will be played at Golden State on Saturday night as each team seeks its first WNBA championship. After having their lowest scoring games of the Finals in losses in Games 4 and 5, the Dream enjoyed an offensive awakening when faced with the must-win mandate. On Wednesday, the Dream announced a sellout for Game 6 despite the much-criticized 12:30 p.m. ET tipoff. There were only scattered empty seats in the upper level despite concerns about work and school obligations hurting the turnout. Angel Reese recorded a double-double with 15 points and 13 rebounds for Atlanta. Gabby Williams led the Valkyries with 26 points. Tiffany Hayes added 15. Valkyries Playoffs 16 hours ago Golden State Valkyries 19 hours ago Atlanta’s biggest lead was 25 points. The Valkyries stormed back in the final minutes, pulling to 77-66 on Laeticia Amihere’s two free throws with 1:57 remaining. After being held to 22 points in the first half of their 65-55 loss in Game 5, the Dream matched that total in the first 6:30 of the opening quarter. Much of the production came on 3s. Atlanta made 6 of 8 3s and 11 of 15 shots overall while racing to a 32-15 lead in the first quarter. After leading 6-5, the Dream pulled away with 13 unanswered points in a run that included two 3s from Jordin Canada. Reese joined the 3-point party with a shot from the corner in the second period. Entering the game, the Dream were 15-0 when Reese had at least one 3. While Atlanta’s sharp shooting continued for a 46-26 halftime lead, the Valkyries struggled. Golden State made only 9 of 34 shots in the half, often struggling to create open opportunities because of the Dream’s smothering defense. Howard opened the second half with another 3-pointer. Valkyries guard Veronica Burton was called for a flagrant foul later midway through the third period when an officials’ review determined she made an unnecessary windup and contact on Howard’s face as Howard was driving for a basket. Kaila Charles closed the third quarter with a 3-pointer for Golden State that trimmed Atlanta’s lead to 16 points at 63-47. It was the smallest lead for the Dream since the 13-0 run in the opening period. Golden State pulled to within 13 points at 68-55 before Gray and Reese sank 3s to push the lead to 74-55. Williams’ three-point play cut the led to 77-69 before Gray sank a crucial 3-pointer for Atlanta. Hayes was called for her fifth foul in a collision for a loose ball with 5:01 remaining. Hayes left the court slowly after receiving attention from a trainer.

headlines.title: Young girls skip school with their parents to attend Valkyries' early WNBA Finals watch party
headlines.description: Sika Lopez took 11-year-old daughter Kendra out of school Thursday to be part of the early morning watch party outside Chase Center cheering for the Golden State Valkyries. Lopez grew up in Los Angeles watching Lisa Leslie and the Sparks, and believes being present can impact Kendra chasing her own dreams — so they joined several thousand fans gathering on the plaza at Thrive City outside Chase Center to support Golden State in Game 6 of the WNBA Finals at Atlanta. “This is such a monumental moment. The Valkyries have worked so hard. When I was her age this wasn’t even possible,” Sika said between clapping along with the others. “Lisa Leslie growing up, she was larger than life.” The Valkyries lost 80-69 as Atlanta forced a winner-take-all Game 7 back in the Bay Area on Saturday. It will be the first seventh game in WNBA Finals history, and one team will capture its first championship. The loss hardly kept Golden State fans from celebrating what this means for women’s basketball in the Bay Area and far beyond. Wendy Franklin-Willis and longtime friend Liz Shaw couldn’t wait for one more. “She played hooky for this,” Shaw said of Franklin-Willis, a middle school teacher in the East Bay suburb of Castro Valley. “I love the community and we’re behind the Valkyries. No matter what happens.” Added Franklin-Willis: “They’ve already won by getting here, a second-year expansion team, no real superstar, such the way the game should be played, and here they are, a game away.” WNBA 18 hours ago Valkyries Playoffs 16 hours ago “This is incredible,” Franklin-Willis said. “You have two teams, Atlanta’s been to the final but has never won, you have two teams with young players. You have the misfit, poised Valkyries against Atlanta, yeah, amazing.” Earlier, hundreds of hands raised when energetic in-arena host Ari Waller asked if fans had taken a day off work or school to attend the violet-clad watch party, where fans received rally towels upon entry and Violet the beloved raven “bestie” — no, she’s not a mascot — danced and posed for photos. Kendra Lopez missed a day of sixth grade in the East Bay to root on the Valkyries and her favorite player, Kayla Thornton. “It makes a big difference because the Valkyries are such a young team and to be able to support them so early means something to me,” Kendra said. Joshua Padilla from Santa Clara felt the same way, bringing his two daughters to San Francisco — 15-year-old high school sophomore Mariah and 10-year-old Malia, who is in fifth grade. Both girls told their teachers they had doctor appointments, along the lines of what point guard Veronica Burton had suggested when she noted after Game 5, “Call in sick, I recommend it.” “It’s just really special. I’m happy to be here with my sister and my dad, we never really get the quality time,” Mariah said. “I think this is a great way, something we all connect with and we love the Valkyries.” Despite the early hour and some frustrated supporters about the scrutinized early tipoff time at 9:30 a.m. PDT, “Ballhalla” braved commuter traffic to be in place for this event and watch the game on the big screen, which is 74 feet wide and 42 feet high. Though the Valkyries trailed 46-26 at halftime, being part of this memorable scene meant far more than the score in a game that finished before lunch time on the West Coast. For Padilla, he knows how important it is to expose his daughters to powerful, athletic women not to mention all of the diversity in the Valkyries’ fan base. They considered it a great day no matter who won. “That’s exactly why I wanted to have them come out here, women’s sports is thriving right now and it’s becoming bigger,” he said. “I actually have four daughters, so being able to come with two of them and support the women and women’s sports it just shows them that it’s up and coming and there’s something to strive for later on down the road.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: How NASA Ames' lunar landing simulator helps prepare for moon missions
headlines.description: The United States is going back to the moon. Part of the training goes through the Bay Area, where the NASA Ames Research Center has a lunar landing simulator. The simulator is a system of motors, hydraulics and technology that serves as a crucial testing platform. It allows pilots and astronauts to simulate a landing on the moon, as well as a boat or shuttle launch or another kind of spacecraft. Astronauts have used the platform before countless expeditions into space. NBC Bay Area’s Scott Budman got the chance to strap in on Thursday and give it a ride. Watch his full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Former Oakland city employees testify in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: Former Oakland city employees took the stand on Thursday in the Sheng Thao federal corruption trial. Latonda Simmons, Oakland’s former assistant city administrator, testified that former Mayor Sheng Thao asked her to become city administrator if she won the mayor’s race. Simmons said she was disappointed when Thao appointed Harold Duffy interim city administrator. Simmons said she also felt excluded from homelessness discussions during the time of the alleged corruption scheme. Defense attorneys questioned Simmons’ motives for testifying, pointing to her grievances with Thao and other city employees. Simmons acknowledged doing her own investigation after the feds searched Thao’s house, and sharing research with prosecutors on what she believed was a broader conspiracy. Sheng Thao Oct 28 Sheng Thao Oct 27 Sheng Thao Oct 26 Sheng Thao Oct 23 Former city administrator Jestin Johnson also took the stand and testified about a meeting with businessmen David Duong and Mario Juarez. Johnson said Thao and her chief of staff asked him to meet with the Duongs about their recycling company, California Waste Solutions. But he testified the discussion turned to modular housing through Duong’s other company, Evolutionary Homes, including a proposal by the businessmen to bypass the normal city contract approval process. Johnson said the units were too expensive and stressed any homeless housing solutions contract would require a competitive proposal process open to other companies. On cross-examination, he acknowledged Thao often asked him to meet with community members and business owners. Prosecutors allege Thao and her boyfriend, Andre Jones, conspired with the Duongs to help get her elected mayor in exchange for granting them city contracts and a commitment to buy the housing units. The government’s key witness Mario Juarez is expected to take the stand on Friday for his highly anticipated testimony. Juarez, deemed a co-conspirator by prosecutors, previously pleaded guilty in the case.
